🌷 Hanoi’s Flower Bicycles — A Moving Piece of the City

One of the most beautiful things you’ll notice while wandering through Hanoi is the flower bicycles passing quietly through the streets. 🚲🌸

Loaded with seasonal flowers, these colorful bicycles bring a little piece of Hanoi’s countryside into the heart of the city.

From lotus and chrysanthemums to sunflowers and roses, each season brings a different display of colors. And if you spot one in the early morning, with the old streets still quiet and soft sunlight shining through… that’s a very Hanoi moment. ✨

📍 Best spots: Hanoi Old Quarter, West Lake, French Quarter
⏰ Best time: Early morning

Your Hanoi food walk starts here 🍜🇻🇳

Got one afternoon in Hanoi? Follow this route through the Old Quarter and taste some local favorites along the way 👇

☕ 1. Café Giảng — 39 Nguyễn Hữu Huân
Start with Hanoi’s famous egg coffee — strong Vietnamese coffee topped with a rich, creamy egg foam.

🥖 2. Bánh Mì 25 — 25 Hàng Cá
Crispy baguette, pâté, meat, fresh herbs and sauce. Quick, easy, and perfect while exploring the Old Quarter.

🍢 3. Ấu Triệu — near St. Joseph’s Cathedral
Grab a tiny plastic chair and try Hanoi-style afternoon snacks like nem chua rán, fries and lemon tea.

🍜 4. Phở Bát Đàn — 49 Bát Đàn
Time for a Hanoi classic: phở bò with fragrant broth, rice noodles and tender beef.

🍦 5. Kem Tràng Tiền — 35 Tràng Tiền
End the walk with one of Hanoi’s nostalgic favorites. Grab an ice cream and stroll toward Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

📍 Café Giảng → Bánh Mì 25 → Ấu Triệu → Phở Bát Đàn → Kem Tràng Tiền
🚶 3–5 hours | Mostly walking

💸 YOUR HANOI MONEY GUIDE (SAVE THIS BEFORE YOUR TRIP) 🇻🇳

One thing that surprises many first-time visitors in Vietnam?

The amount of zeros on our money 😂

Here are a few things you should know:

💵 Cash is still useful
Small cafés, street food stalls, and local shops may prefer cash.

👀 Watch the zeros
20,000₫ and 200,000₫ look similar… but they are VERY different 😅

💬 Useful phrase:
“Bao nhiêu tiền?” = How much?

Don’t worry — after a few days, Vietnamese Dong becomes much easier to understand.

🚦 GOING TO VIETNAM? HERE’S A HIDDEN SKILL YOU NEED TO UNLOCK:

Crossing the road.

In Vietnam’s big cities, motorbikes move like a never-ending river. 
The first time you see it, you might freeze and think:

“Okay... but HOW am I supposed to get across?”

The secret is actually simple:

🚶 Walk slowly and steadily. 
Don’t suddenly stop. Don’t run. 
Keep watching the traffic, use crossings when you can, and let the flow move around you.

It feels chaotic at first, but once you find the rhythm, it weirdly starts to make sense.

The first time you cross the street looking calm, confident, and totally unbothered?

✨ That’s when you know you’re finally getting Vietnam.  #travelmoments  #travelframe #vietnam

Train Street rules tourists should know before you go.

This is a real working railway running through a residential neighbourhood, not a guaranteed tourist attraction. Access can change without notice, so never plan your day around an old TikTok schedule or a “guaranteed entry” promise.

Here is how to visit responsibly:
1. Respect barriers and instructions
  If police, railway staff, or local authorities ask you to leave, leave immediately. Do not try another entrance or argue your way in.
2. Do not stand, sit, or pose on the tracks
  The train can arrive faster than you expect. Keep your whole body, phone, bag, tripod, and loose clothing away from the railway corridor.
3. Do not trust crowds as a safety signal
  A busy café does not mean it is safe to sit close to the tracks. Skip the shot if there is not enough space.
4. Do not rely on online train times
  Schedules and access rules can change. Treat any timetable you see online as a guide only, never as permission to enter.
5. Remember: people live here
  Keep noise low, do not block homes or businesses, and never move furniture for your photo.

The best Hanoi memories are the ones you can enjoy safely and respectfully.

5 Hanoi scams tourists still fall for, and how to handle them without ruining your day.

Hanoi is warm, vibrant, and very welcoming. These are simply a few moments where staying calm and clear can save you money and awkward conversations:
1. Uninvited shoe repair
  If someone starts handling your shoes, say “Khong, cam on” and keep walking. Do not let a “quick fix” turn into a surprise bill.
2. Fruit basket photo trap
  That cute photo with a shoulder pole or fruit basket may come with an unexpected charge. Ask first, or just smile and decline.
3. Unofficial taxis
  Use a ride-hailing app or a reputable taxi. Always match the plate, driver, and fare before getting in.
4. Cash and change confusion
  Vietnamese notes can look similar when you are rushing. Say the denomination out loud, keep your note visible, and count your change.
5. No agreed price for a ride
  Before a cyclo or motorbike ride, ask: “What is the total price for the whole ride?” Agree first, ride second.

Save this before paying with cash in Hanoi. 🚨

Vietnam is one of the friendliest and safest country to explore, but these street tricks are surprisingly easy to fall for.

Here’s what to watch out for:
1️⃣ The cash swap 💸
Vietnamese notes can look surprisingly similar:
• 500,000 VND and 20,000 VND are both blue
• 200,000 VND and 10,000 VND have similar reddish-orange colours
You hand over 500k, the seller swaps it for 20k and claims you underpaid. Easy fix: hold the note up and say the amount out loud before handing it over.
2️⃣ The surprise shoe repair 👟
Someone starts cleaning or gluing your shoes without asking, then demands a huge fee. Say “KHÔNG” firmly and keep walking.
3️⃣ The fruit basket photo 🍍
That cute bamboo-basket photo might come with a not-so-cute bill. Ask the price before touching or accepting anything.
4️⃣ Sketchy taxi meters 🚖
Avoid unmarked taxis. Use Grab or a trusted transfer service so you can see the price before getting in.
5️⃣ Train Street “entrance fees” 🚂

Be careful if someone claims you must pay them to enter. Follow current local rules and arrange a seat directly with a trackside cafe instead.

Vietnam is still one of the friendliest places we’ve travelled. Just remember: not every “free” street experience is actually free. 😅
